title_original: Walston, A New Space for Photography in the Scottish Hills
excerpt_original: Walston is a new photographic center housed in a 17th-century church in the heart of Scotland founded by Caroline Kenyon. Cet article Walston, A New Space for Photography in the Scottish Hills est apparu en premier sur The Eye of Photography Magazine .

blocks.text: Founder of the World Food Photography Awards, a leading food photography competition, Caroline Kenyon is pursuing her commitment to photography through a long-held ambition: Walston, a gallery housed in a 17th-century church in the heart of Scotland. An interview about turning this distinctive place into a new destination for photography.
Can you tell us about your first encounter with this church? How did you discover it, and what drew you to it?

During the Covid-19 pandemic, I was in London, looking after my elderly mother with my brother. In the evenings, I would browse online and discovered that many rural churches in Scotland were being put up for sale. It revived my hope of one day having a space in which to create a gallery, something I had dreamed of for many years.

When I was able to return home, I spotted a beautiful church for sale. I arranged a viewing, travelling by train, bus and taxi, and as soon as I saw its magnificent setting, standing alone at the edge of a valley in the vast Pentland Hills, I thought this was a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity. All the windows except one were boarded up, yet the place was still filled with light. It had a powerful, beautiful atmosphere. I spent fifteen minutes there and called the agent to make an offer.
How did you adapt the space, or decide not to adapt it, to turn a 17th-century church into Walston, a photography gallery?

It has undergone very light restoration. I wanted to preserve the magical, Sleeping Beauty atmosphere it had when I first found it. There is no electricity or running water and, for now, I have no plans to change that. There are two spaces: the main one is over 15 metres long and forms the gallery, with chalk-white walls, while the small vestry will be painted red and become a warm, comfortable office. The building is so distinctive and its setting extraordinary: there are beautiful graves and monuments in the churchyard, nothing unsettling, just something peaceful and lovely.
You mention on social media that the opening is just days away. What do the final preparations look like?

Everything is gathering pace! The decorator is painting tirelessly, I have rolls of film to collect and take to Edinburgh for developing and scanning, the local fine-art printer will make the prints, we have framing to do, and much more. But it is such an exciting thing to undertake, and I am genuinely touched by the enthusiasm and support of the whole local community. I am staying in the nearby town of Biggar, in a family-run pub, and whenever I walk in after the long drive, I feel at home. I want people to feel that this is their space too. It is a place that needs to be treated with care and respect. And I hope the opening will be a truly joyful celebration of the affection people feel for a beautiful place, with photography, tea and cakes. A real party.
Can you tell us more about the first exhibition, which will be closely connected to the place and its surroundings?

It was very important to me that the inaugural exhibition should be rooted in the community. So I approached the Biggar & District Men’s Shed to propose a photography workshop for its members, with the resulting work forming the opening exhibition. It was Henry, my photographer son, who suggested that the men focus on their fellow members’ hands as they repair, make and restore things, to keep the subject and theme specific, and that they work on film, which I loved.
You have said, ‘I have always wanted a space to show work that matters to me and that I think will matter to others.’ Does this feel like an artistic dream coming true?

I have been looking at photographs all my life. My mother was a journalist who wrote for The Observer and The Times, and when I was very young she would show me photographs by the great Jane Bown and Lord Snowdon. When I was in my twenties, editing a magazine I described as a low-budget National Geographic, I saw every photographer’s portfolio and made all the picture selections myself.

I developed my eye and my responses to images. That was long before the World Food Photography Awards were established; they are now in their 16th year. I have the privilege of sitting on the shortlisting jury and seeing every image submitted, thousands each year. I work alongside experienced colleagues, from photographers and creative directors to editors, and have learned a great deal from them.
What would you like to show and create in this space? Do you already have ideas or plans for future exhibitions?

I have a long list of potential future exhibitions! Next June, I am planning an exhibition by Clive Boursnell, the great garden photographer, featuring images of Little Sparta, one of Scotland’s most celebrated gardens, created by the late artist Ian Hamilton Finlay, which happens to be just across the valley. I had no idea it was there when I made my offer on the church.

I am gathering the names of photographers whose work I would like to show. I find ideas everywhere, through conversations and chance encounters. And sometimes it is work by people with extraordinary talent who do not think of themselves as photographers. It is a great pleasure to give them a little encouragement and a platform to show their work.

There are themes too: the World Food Photography Awards will collaborate with Photo Dalkeith in 2028, which is very exciting, and I am planning a parallel exhibition at Walston devoted to ice cream, using images from the Awards’ archive. Ice cream is a great Scottish tradition, also connected to the history of Italians who settled in Scotland more than a century ago and opened ice cream businesses, many of which are still there today. A lovely way to bring different strands together.
